Graph of a Polynomial Defined by Its Roots

AlgebraCurvesParity
Game: Build a curve from the points where it should meet the middle line, and see how it bends.
How to play: Change the numbers in the formula, or pick how many there are. Watch where the curve crosses the line and where it only touches it.

Look for the math

Write a polynomial as a product, P(x) = A(x − r₁)(x − r₂)…(x − rₙ), and its roots are on show: P(r) = 0 exactly when one of the factors is 0. A few general rules then tell you the shape of the graph before you draw it.

At the two ends

Far from 0 every factor x − r has the sign of x, so P(x) has the sign of A·xⁿ. On the right that is the sign of A. On the left it depends on the parity of the degree: with A positive,

odd degree: −∞ on the left, +∞ on the right
even degree: +∞ on both sides

and with A negative the signs flip. Changing A stretches the graph up and down; changing its sign reflects it in the x-axis. The test checked the table and the stretching on all 4,686 polynomials of degree up to 4 with roots from −2 to 2 and A from −3 to 3.

Crossing or touching

Near a root r that appears m times, P(x) behaves like a constant times (x − r)ᵐ. If the multiplicity m is odd, that changes sign and the graph crosses the axis (a filled dot); if m is even it does not, and the graph touches the axis and turns back (a ring). Whenever m > 1, odd or even, the graph is tangent to the axis there, because the derivative also has the factor x − r. The page's wording "tangent regardless of the root's parity" means the multiplicity's parity; the test confirmed all of these on the same polynomials.

Make all three roots the same number. The curve flattens as it crosses. Now make two of them equal and the third different: where does it cross, and where does it touch?

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
